news.title: National groups ramp up spending in rural AZ congressional district
news.text:
It would be tough for Democrats to flip one of Arizona's rural, conservative-leaning congressional districts this year, but that hasn't stopped national political groups from pouring in money.

Both parties are funneling resources into the seat held by incumbent Republican Rep. Eli Crane as polling suggests Republicans could face serious headwinds in this year's midterms.

Crane won reelection in Arizona's 2nd Congressional District by nearly 10 points in 2024, roughly 55%-45%.

He is now locked in a rematch against the same Democratic candidate, former Navajo Nation President Jonathan Nez.

The district, which includes a large swath of northeastern Arizona, favors Republicans and historically has voted for President Donald Trump by double-digit margins. But the uptick in spending is a sign both parties are keeping tabs on the district during a midterm cycle that could be challenging for the GOP.

"I would still categorize it as a reach opportunity," said Erin Covey, an analyst with the non-partisan Cook Political Report. "Democrats do have a credible path to victory, even if it is narrow."

Race heats up, at least on paper

The race appears to be heating up, at least on paper.

Crane and Nez have ramped up their fundraising since the last election cycle.

The size of Crane's campaign war chest has roughly doubled since 2024, records show. He has received more than $800,000 from House Republican leaders, a steep increase from years past. Nez, too, is bringing in more cash, raising about four times as much money compared to 2024.

But Crane's campaign still had the edge heading into August. He had raised about twice as much as Nez in total and spent four times as much.

Outside groups have been mobilizing in the district. Several Democratic-aligned groups have spent more than $750,000 in an ongoing attack ad campaign targeting the congressman, a sizable spend with more than two months to go before the election.

Non-partisan political analysts still rate the race as "likely" safe for Republicans.

Covey said the spending patterns mirror what's happening in other races where Republicans have a modest advantage. It makes sense for Democrats to start spending money, she said, but it might be more of a trial balloon to see how effective their attacks are, and whether it's worth investing even more money into the district as November approaches.

Arizona district becoming a priority

Democrats have emphasized that Nez performed several points better than their party's presidential candidate Kamala Harris in the district during the 2024 cycle, raising liberal hopes of an upset victory. Even if Nez repeats that strong performance, he still has a lot of ground to make up. The district strongly favored Trump during the 2020 and 2024 presidential cycles, illustrating its Republican tilt.

Liberal spenders hope this campaign cycle will bring new opportunities.

The recent attack ads, a joint effort by the League of Conservation Voters and a Latino voter engagement group, have highlighted Crane's opposition to clean energy tax credits in an attempt to win over voters who are concerned about their energy bills.

Nez's campaign has elevated pocketbook issues.

"Regardless of the money Crane and his billionaire friends will pour in this election season to deceive Arizona voters, Nez is focused on a campaign built on protecting our water, lowering costs, improving infrastructure, and taking our government back from the hands of the elites," Mark Hatton, a campaign spokesperson, wrote in a statement to The Republic.

Crane, for his part, has leaned into some rural Arizonans' skepticism of clean-energy projects, railing against "green new deal" policymaking and describing large wind and solar farms as being driven by "corporate elites." He's also promoted the Republican-led tax cut package he helped pass last year.

"Selling out rural Arizonans to avoid a third straight electoral loss is a bold strategy by Mr. Nez," wrote Greg Smith, a Crane spokesperson.

His district isn't at the top of the GOP's list of priorities. About two dozen seats, including two in Arizona, are generally regarded as much more competitive and have seen significantly more spending by both political parties.

The clearest sign of the district's competitiveness will be if national Republican Party groups mobilize to defend Crane, said Covey, like they're doing in the top battleground seats. But that hasn't happened yet.

"If they actually come and insert spending here, then we'll know he is truly vulnerable," she said.
news.author: The Arizona Republic

news.title: Is Trump dragging Republicans down?
news.text:
It’s the Democrats who have mostly had to answer questions about electability this midterm season, but why are there so few questions about the “E” word for the other side?
Gas prices are still skyrocketing. A number of Republican candidates, such as Ohio Rep. Max Miller and former Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who’s running for a Senate seat, are mired in scandal. The Iran war was unpopular from the start, but it is getting even less popular as it drags on. And Trump’s approval rating recently hit 33 percent, the lowest of his presidency yet.
On this week’s episode of America, Actually, host Astead Herndon speaks with one of Trump’s most vocal defenders, conservative influencer CJ Pearson, about whether we’re seeing Trump’s brand slip even among his supporters and the young people who helped him win in 2024, and how that could affect the midterm elections. 
Pearson, a conservative content creator and influencer, first went viral when he posted himself, then 12 years old, criticizing Barack Obama in a YouTube video. Now 24, Pearson is one of MAGA’s most prominent Black voices.
In this episode, Astead and Pearson discussed how Republicans should answer questions about whether voters’ lives are better than they were two years ago; whether Trump still has any cultural cachet left over from his last presidential campaign; and when Pearson started to see young Republicans turning away from the MAGA movement.
Below is an excerpt of Astead’s conversation with Pearson, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel.
[Media: https://open.spotify.com/show/0xv3qPaQ9tu0l5zyz7AQkx?si=2d127db4ff3644af]
That “E” word’s been thrown around a lot about Democrats, but we want to think about how Republicans are on their own. If you could rate Donald Trump’s second term one through 10, what would you give it?
I think the president’s doing incredibly well for the American people. Promises made, promises kept in many ways. 
I think if you look at this president who ran on securing our southern border, he’s done it. You look at this president who’s talked about bringing down costs, he’s brought down the cost of dairy, eggs. He’s achieved that. 
And I think also this president is only just getting started. He ran on “no tax on tips.” He did that. He ran on “no tax on overtime.” He did that. Oftentimes I tell people the challenge of this administration is keeping up the messaging at the same pace as the accomplishments of this president.
And so I think that there’s a lot more work to do. Thankfully, we have two more years to do it.
Can I get a number?
I think he’s doing well. I will say I grew up in a place where there’s always room for improvement, so I’ll give him an eight.
You’re giving him an eight. I wanted to just start there because Trump’s approval rating has fallen, as I’m sure you have seen. Why do you think the country isn’t maybe on the same page as you?
I think a lot of people are focused on their pocketbooks, right? They’re focused on domestic issues, and I think that we have been very internationally focused over the course of the past few months as we’ve navigated and dealt with the Iran conflict. 
But I think that as we get ready to get through this last wave of primaries, I think you’re going to see a change in his messaging and a reset at the midterm convention in Dallas next month in September. 
And I think you’re going to hear this president talking about how he’s made America more affordable, how he’s kept Americans safe, far safer than they were under President Joe Biden.
And I think that you’ll see those numbers start to change. And a reminder, the only poll that matters is on Election Day. There are many polls that had Kamala Harris beating President Trump, in 2024, and that didn’t happen.
Yeah, I don’t want to be overly poll-reliant, but we’ve heard some of this directly from Republicans even. 
We were at Donald Trump’s UFC event in DC talking to young men, and even there we heard people really come to be critical on three issues specifically: tariffs, the Iran war, and the handling of the Epstein files.
You mentioned the question of affordability. Donald Trump has said, quote, “I love the inflation.” And when asked by reporters about the public strain that has come from the conflicts with Iran, he said, “I don’t think about Americans’ financial situation. I don’t think about anybody.”
How can you say that Republicans are gonna run on affordability if the president’s saying he doesn’t care if Americans’ lives are unaffordable?
Well, I’ve often said that we can’t cede this entire affordability debate to the Democrats. The reason that I think a lot of young people are giving a little bit, even a flirtatious nod to the DSA and their socialist and communist candidates, is because they’re talking about an issue that’s top of mind for them.
In the same way that when President Trump won in 2024, he was talking about issues that were top of mind of the American voter, which was the cost of living. 
And so I think that we need to get back to that messaging. I think that this president has continued to deliver on that front. Costs are coming down.
The economy is resurging. We’re seeing economic and global investment in this country unlike anything we’ve seen before. In Oklahoma, we’re bringing back manufacturing with the aluminum smelting plant.
But the president’s not saying this. The president’s saying, “I love the inflation, and I don’t think about Americans’ financial situation.” Do those words help Republican midterm candidates?
Well, I think the president has a lot of time to say a lot more things because Election Day is pretty far away from now. I think we have two or three months left, and I think the president will make this case. 
But I think what will also make the case is that the candidates that the Democrats are running and nominating all across this country, who are now affiliating themselves with the socialist movement, are not actually fighting for things that will actually ever work.
Socialism has never worked anywhere it’s been tried, and I think that this is going to be an election between common sense versus crazy. Do you wanna run a candidate that hates Thanksgiving?
For the record, that candidate lost in the primary. She will not be on the ballot in November.
She did. She almost was there, though, and that’s the thing. I’m glad common sense won the day in Wisconsin, that the good people there love turkey.
I know that you say that the argument is based on how Democrats are out of touch, but we have talked about some ways in which Donald Trump has not lived up to folks’ expectations, particularly on things like prices and on things like the Iran war.
How does the GOP overcome that electability question? What is their message when folks ask, is their life better than two years ago?
I think we’ve got to lock in. I think we also need to prosecute the case that it’s going to be a lot worse under the Democrats if these crazy communists get into office. And so I think that when you’re looking at costs, we need to make that argument central. We need to make that what we lead with.
And I think that we have to pump the brakes on a lot of the international stuff. And I think that we need to talk about the things that are actually affecting people’s everyday lives at grocery stores, at gas stations, wherever it may be. And I think that is how we can kind of turn the ship around.
When we talk about the Democratic candidates, you’re saying the DSA candidates are far left, and we’ve certainly explored some electability questions for them and some ways that I think they might have stances that are misaligned with the American people. But so does Donald Trump, and he’s endorsed scandal-plagued candidates like Ken Paxton in Texas, like Max Miller in Ohio.
Why is that not just as much a sign of a conservative version of extremism, just as you are arguing that there’s a Democratic or leftist version of that?
Because I think you’re talking about folks who have dealt with issues in their personal lives, not necessarily their voting record.
Okay, maybe I should say Tom Tiffany, who didn’t vote to certify the 2020 election, but I imagine you agree with him.
Well, no, I think that was six years ago. I don’t think about 2020 anymore. I think about 2026 and I think about 2028. So when I look at that … it’s important that we really make the case for crazy communism versus common sense. And I think that the American people are not going to vote for that.
I guess I’m saying, does Donald Trump win the commonsense argument? Like, isn’t crazy versus commonsense an argument that Democrats can make and say Donald Trump is said crazy?
No, because I think Donald Trump definitely wins the common sense argument when we’re running against folks who belong to a party that is now, you know, waging a war against Thanksgiving, who believe that biological men should be playing women’s sports. Again, these are 80/20 issues, and so I actually really like our odds here.
It’s going to be hard, right? It’s always hard for the party that controls the White House to fare all too well in any midterm election. But I think that we’re going to overperform. I think we’re going to hold onto the Senate. The House will be a dogfight, but I like our chances.

news.title: A Bayh-gone era for Indiana Democrats?
news.text:
Now it’s one of Evan Bayh’s sons, Beau Bayh, seeking office in Indiana. On Aug. 8 at Potawatomi Park in South Bend, Beau Bayh delivered a kick-out-the-bums rallying cry to regular applause from 150 or so Democratic activists and local candidates. Beau Bayh, 30, is running for Indiana’s secretary of state — seeking not only his father’s political starter job from four decades ago but also trying to resurrect the moribund Democratic brand in the Hoosier State.

It’s been 14 years since Democrats won a statewide race in Indiana. Since then, Republicans have cemented control of both Senate seats, the governor’s office, overwhelming supermajorities in the state’s House and Senate, and no less than a White House-led effort to eliminate the state’s remaining two Democratic members of Congress (which was its own source of chaotic drama). President Donald Trump won Indiana in 2024 by 59% to 40% over Democratic rival Kamala Harris. 

So, in the wilderness and under siege, the state’s remaining Democratic Party brass set their sights on Birch Evans “Beau” Bayh IV to spark something close to a renaissance. All from the office that oversees election administration and business licensing.

In other words, no pressure.

A three-way race

Speaking just off to the side from the picnic tables filled with activists, Bayh told the Washington Examiner he was called to public service by a desire to help and to clean out the corruption he said has grown in the past four years.

“I was raised in a family of public servants, and I was always taught growing up that no one forces you to run for public office, but if you decide to do that, you ought to do it to help your community, your state, and your country,” Beau Bayh said before taking the mic at the St. Joseph’s County Democrats third annual Picnic in the Park. “When I see the current secretary of state use his position of trust with the public, his office, not as it means to benefit our state, as it means to benefit himself, that kind of offends my sense of what a public servant should be.”

In any normal situation, the race would be a cakewalk for the candidate with the “R” next to their name.

But a whirlwind of state and national scandals, a chaotic intraparty Republican fight, and the emergence of a third-party wild card — as well as interviews with more than two dozen Indiana Democratic and Republican operatives over the last few months — give the impression Beau Bayh could indeed win in November. 

Indiana’s secretary of state is rarely a blockbuster race, but in the absence of a governor’s race or top-tier Senate battle, it’s the main draw. The (limited) publicly available data reveal a surprising three-way showdown between Bayh, Republican Max Engling — a former congressional aide and losing 2024 House candidate — and former Indianapolis Mayor Greg Ballard, running as an independent under the banner of his newly created Lincoln Party.

Bayh had $2.3 million in the bank at the end of June. Engling is sitting on a meager $15,000 after a late entry (more on that in a second). And Ballard has raised and spent close to $1 million, according to numbers compiled by the Indiana Capital Chronicle.

Beau Bayh looks comfortable working the crowd, talking with older Democrats long sold on the Bayh brand dating back to Birch Bayh’s time in office and younger activists with barely a memory of the Bayh family reign. 

“We need leaders here in our state that recognize that what we have in common as Americans and Hoosiers will always be more important than the little things they try and use to divide us amongst each other,” Bayh told the crowd. “I know, some folks here today might call me naive. I get it. I see this vitriol in our politics, I’m subjected to it myself, as is every brave person who’s had the courage to put their name on the ballot here this fall.”

At his back is a strong team of Indiana veterans and national Democratic operatives with Hoosier ties, including Mike Schmuhl, an architect of Pete Buttigieg’s rise from South Bend mayor with an unpronounceable last name to standout national Democratic star. 

“Beau is an excellent candidate,” said Schmuhl, a senior adviser to Beau Bayh and veteran Indiana Democratic leader. “He’s doing all the right things. He’s very disciplined. He has a professional team. He’s taking it very seriously. He’s raising the resources to win a statewide race in Indiana, something we haven’t done obviously since 2012.”

But the state’s Democratic Party infrastructure, which was built on a framework of union workers, teachers, and rural and urban coalitions, has been gutted in recent decades through a mix of factory closures, offshoring, and strategic cuts to union and teacher support by the state’s dominant Republican Party.

Coming out of the summer, Beau Bayh looks in a surprisingly strong position, but the fall homestretch appears to be a grueling battle. 

Bayh and his team built a strategy of running against the state’s unpopular incumbent Republican Secretary of State Diego Morales, who allegedly used tax dollars to buy a $90,000 GMC Yukon Denali from a dealer who donated to his campaign, traveled the globe on secret trips, and kicked up a steady storm of mini-scandals. 

Just days before the filing deadline, the state’s new GOP powerbrokers, Sen. Jim Banks (R-IN) and Attorney General Todd Rokita, called for Morales to leave the race. After he refused, they helped former congressional staffer Engling oust Morales at the state party convention.

Engling, a new Republican candidate with a clean record and strong ties in Washington and Indiana — not unlike Beau Bayh himself — entered the race late with an initial fundraising deficit. 

But all expectations are that fundraising will pick up easily for the new candidate, not least because of his strong ties to former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy, a GOP fundraising juggernaut.

Still a red state

Republicans are confident they’ll have plenty of material to blast Beau Bayh with as the fall campaign heats up, starting with what critics call Beau Bayh’s rather tenuous ties to Indiana.

Bayh was born in Indianapolis when his father was governor. After Evan Bayh was elected to the Senate in 1998, the family moved to Washington, D.C. Beau Biden graduated from St. Albans School and then Harvard College. He was then commissioned in the Marine Corps and deployed to Europe following the Russian invasion of Ukraine. He was honorably discharged at the rank of captain in 2023. 

Bayh earned a Juris Doctor from Harvard Law School and moved to Westfield, Indiana, to study for the bar exam in 2024. After passing, he clerked for a federal appeals court judge and then joined an Indianapolis law firm. 

Indiana connections to Bayh family members have already proven a political liability. Evan Bayh’s ill-fated 2016 Senate comeback bid, after six years out of office, was undone in no small part by attacks that he was too much Washington and had forgotten his Hoosier roots. This was punctuated by an Indianapolis Star investigation that showed neighbors at his Indianapolis condo rarely, if ever, saw him.

And the “carpetbagger” attack has already been primed in a tough intraparty Democratic battle in which Army veteran Blythe Potter’s supporters roundly knocked Beau Bayh as an elite Ivy League product of Washington with little connection to Indiana beyond his last name. (Beau Bayh beat Potter at the state party convention 1,385 to 883 — hardly a knockout.)

W. JAMES ANTLE: DOES ANYONE WANT TO WIN THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS?

The wild card for Beau Bayh and the GOP’s Engling, ironically, is the surprisingly well-funded third-party bid of Ballard. He was Indianapolis’s mayor from 2008 to 2016, as a Republican. He joined the secretary of state’s race as an independent amid mounting reports of corruption by Morales, the GOP incumbent. 

For Beau Bayh and the state’s Democrats seeking an institutional foothold, they’re now bracing for a flood of money for Engling and a subsequent wave of attacks in the final months of the race. 

Tom LoBianco is editor and co-founder of 24sight News, based in Silver Spring, Maryland. He is the author of the biography about President Donald Trump’s first vice president, Piety & Power: Mike Pence and the Taking of the White House, and was an Indiana statehouse reporter for the Associated Press.

news.title: NABJ says Stephen A. Smith crossed the line. What line? | Opinion
news.text:
Stephen A. Smith may be the most popular sports commentator in America. He's smart. Extremely opinionated. Loud. And he knows how to stir up fans just enough to keep them coming back for more.

He's also done what few sports commentators have been able to do: build a massive multimedia enterprise that extends far beyond simply talking about sports. Yet he has also found himself embroiled in controversy, particularly over his criticism of Black people and, more specifically, women.

His public clashes with U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas), political commentator Joy Reid, former First Lady Michelle Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris helped land Smith on a list no Black journalist wants to make: A 2026 Thumbs Down Award from the National Association of Black Journalists. (Spoiler: I am a long-time NABJ member, but I was not involved in the award.)

NABJ uses the award, established in 1989, to call out individuals, groups and media organizations for reporting, commentary or practices the organization considers insensitive, racist, stereotypical or otherwise contrary to its mission.

I was sitting in the ballroom at NABJ's convention in Atlanta Aug. 15 when Smith's name was announced during the 2026 Salute to Excellence gala. I was there because I had been nominated for two journalism awards. Thankfully, neither was a Thumbs Down Award.

When Smith's name was called, you could feel the reaction. Some journalists sighed. Some laughed. Some clapped. Others seemed genuinely shocked.

I understood why.

Giving that distinction to Smith, a Black journalist who has supported NABJ for decades, was a slap in the face. One of the most prominent organizations of Black journalists was publicly telling one of the most prominent Black voices in media that he had crossed a line.

Opinion: Walker wins without big urban areas is a message to Crowley

Depending on where you stood, that line was either long overdue or dangerously subjective.

The award has been around since 1989, and NABJ says it has been issued 44 times to individuals and institutions. Smith said most recipients have been organizations and that he's only the seventh individual in NABJ history to receive one.

Smith also pointed out that one of those individuals was disgraced former New York Times reporter Jayson Blair, who received the award in 2003. In Smith's view, NABJ had essentially put him in the same company as a journalist whose career collapsed in one of the most notorious plagiarism and fabrication scandals in modern journalism.

Did Stephen A. Smith deserve NABJ's Thumbs Down Award?

Smith wasn't the only recipient. NABJ also gave Thumbs Down Awards to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, CBS News, The Washington Post and DuJuan McCoy, CEO of Circle City Broadcasting.

But Smith was by far the most famous name. So how does one of the most successful Black journalists in America, a man who has supported NABJ and credits the organization with helping his career, end up receiving one of its strongest public rebukes?

The organization pointed to what it described as a pattern of disparaging commentary about prominent Black women. NABJ President Errin Haines said the organization has a responsibility to hold people accountable, regardless of how prominent or successful they are. She said the goal isn't to permanently condemn people or organizations, but to push them to do better.

And that accountability, Haines said, has to include NABJ's friends and allies. If ESPN and Smith support the organization, that shouldn't make them immune from being called out when NABJ believes they've fallen short, in this case a string of comments about Black women, including:

Criticizing Rep. Crockett for what he called “verbiage and rhetoric for the streets” and questioned whether her confrontational approach toward President Donald Trump was helping her constituents. He later apologized.Pointing to Reid's declining ratings after MSNBC canceled her show and questioning whether she should have expected a different outcome. Reid fired back, accusing Smith of being rewarded for saying things about Black people, particularly Black women, that White audiences wanted to hear.Calling out Michelle Obama over comments she made during the 2024 presidential campaign and repeatedly questioned Harris' campaign strategy.

Smith called the award a “personal hit job.” He also blasted NABJ for condemning him without first reaching out to him and giving him an opportunity to respond. He rejects the idea that criticizing prominent Black women means he is disparaging them. His criticism, he argues, has been about their words, politics and public actions, not their race or gender.

I think Smith has a point. As an opinion columnist myself, I believe NABJ went too far.

Of all the examples, Smith's criticism of Crockett troubles me the most. Describing the rhetoric of an accomplished Black congresswoman as being “for the streets” carries racial and gender implications that Smith should have understood.

But Smith also called Crockett educated and brilliant. More importantly, he apologized. That matters.

Can a Black journalist be especially tough on Black women, of Black people in general, without being accused of tearing the Black race down? And who gets to decide when tough commentary crosses that line?

Here's another question: Would Smith have received this award if the people he repeatedly criticized had been Black men?

I don't think so.

Smith goes after Black men all the time. Athletes. Coaches. Executives. Entertainers. He raises his voice, questions their decisions and sometimes says things that make them angry enough to respond publicly.

Sometimes he does go too far, but that's also Stephen A. Smith.

So, if we're going to say Smith crossed a line with Black women, NABJ should be able to show us exactly where that line is. Because criticizing a Black woman isn't the same thing as attacking all Black women.

But what about Smith's tone?

I'm not going to ignore the elephant in the room. The question isn't simply whether Smith criticizes Black women. It's whether his tone changes when he does.

Former ESPN colleague Jemele Hill believes it does. She argues that Smith doesn't always “keep the same energy,” showing more restraint with some critics while becoming much more aggressive with others.

Hill pointed to President Donald Trump as an example. After Smith criticized the disruption caused by Trump's security presence at an NBA Finals game at Madison Square Garden, Trump blasted Smith on Truth Social, calling him “dumb as a rock,” an “arrogant fool” and a “low-IQ individual.”

Yet Hill said people didn't sense the same level of vitriol from Smith toward Trump that they've seen him direct toward some Black women.

That's a fair criticism, and Smith shouldn't dismiss it. But tone is also subjective. What sounds unnecessarily harsh to one person can sound like Stephen A. being Stephen A. to someone else.

He also needs to recognize that his words carry more weight today than they did 20 years ago. He isn't just another sports commentator. He's one of the most powerful Black voices in American media.

That doesn't mean he should go easier on Black women. It means when he turns up the heat on anyone, particularly people from a community he says he cares deeply about, he should understand the impact his words can have.

NABJ believes Smith crossed the line from commentary to cruelty.

Smith wasn't in the ballroom when his name was announced. That may have been a good thing.

Opinion: Fights show we didn't listen after Sherman Park uprising

Because knowing Stephen A., had he been there, he probably would have had plenty to say about NABJ's decision.

And the president of NABJ happens to be a Black woman.

But that doesn't change where I come down.

Smith can be abrasive. He can be wrong. And, yes, sometimes he needs to check his tone.

NABJ has every right to hold Smith accountable, just as Smith has every right to criticize Crockett, Reid, Obama or Harris.

If one of the most prominent organizations of Black journalists is going to give one of the most prominent Black journalists in America an award for commentary it considers harmful to Black women, it should be able to clearly show where legitimate criticism ended and disparagement began.

Hold Smith accountable when he crosses the line. Just make sure there's actually a line before you punish him for crossing it.

The Tories and the Labourites are both in thrall to the radical elements in their parties, which means that they are culturally out of step with average citizens, who are sick and tired of the nation catering to the cost and criminality of illegal immigrants instead of caring for its poorest and weakest.

Events like these rightly disgust the British, which is why the nation is poised to make Farage prime minister in the next general election, no more than three years hence.

How undemocratic is the U.K. these days? Consider that the newest occupant of 10 Downing Street, former Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham, won his seat in Parliament this summer with less than 25,000 votes and was promptly installed as prime minister, replacing the well-meaning but politically inept Keir Starmer. No one was allowed to run against Burnham — shades of Kamala Harris. His not-quite-14,000-vote plurality made Burnham the leader of a nation of 70 million. He was essentially chosen by a miniscule 0.05% of registered U.K. voters. Where’s the democracy in that?

Burnham intends to run the U.K. on the same woke terms as his multitudinous predecessors, which means that it’s only a matter of time before the circular firing squad that is Britain’s Labour Party scuppers him, too, which means Farage’s time is almost here. He has the Trump-like, magical ability to appeal to regular joes, but without much of the Trumpian baggage. He wears his well-spoken everyman identity lightly, still enjoying a pint, a smoke, and a good time.

As the expression says, “There will always be an England.” Yet unless and until Farage takes over, don’t be so sure.

news.title: Medicare for All is back on the ballot
news.text:
Medicare for All is not simply a proposal to let more people buy into Medicare. The current Senate bill, sponsored by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT), would create a federal health plan covering every American, eliminate premiums and cost-sharing, and make it unlawful for existing private and employer plans to exist. Medicare, Medicaid, and the Obamacare exchanges would largely be folded into the new system.

The price tag would be enormous. A 2024 Center for Health and Economy analysis estimated that Kamala Harris’s version of Medicare for All would increase federal spending by $43.9 trillion from 2026 through 2035, while CBO has separately found that similar single-payer systems would dramatically shift health spending onto the federal budget. Meanwhile, the existing Medicare program is projected to exhaust its Hospital Insurance Trust Fund reserves in 2033.

Supporters answer that Americans would no longer pay private premiums. True, but replacing premiums with taxes does not make healthcare free. The federal government would become responsible for financing the entire system.

That is an important caveat to polling. Reuters polling found this month that 60% of independents support “government-provided healthcare.” But that wording does not tell voters what Sanders’s proposal means. Under Medicare for All, Americans could not simply keep their employer plan if they preferred it. Duplicative private insurance would be illegal. Washington would not merely compete with private insurance; it would replace it.

Once government becomes the healthcare monopolist, controlling spending means controlling what providers are paid and, ultimately, how much care is supplied. CBO has found that lower provider payments are the principal source of single-payer savings and warns that increased demand would exceed increased supply, producing “delays and forgone care.”

Britain and Canada show what that reality looks like. England’s National Health Service had over 7 million cases awaiting elective treatment in June, with more than a third waiting longer than 18 weeks and more than 105,000 waiting over a year.

Canada fares little better. In an international survey, 58% of Canadians needing elective surgery waited at least two months, compared with 26% of Americans. Those who can afford to escape sometimes do: One study estimates more than 105,000 Canadians traveled abroad for nonemergency medical care in 2025.

Americans do not need to speculate about whether politicians will accept the taxes needed to build such a system. Vermont already tried. Back in 2014, Democratic Gov. Peter Shumlin abandoned Green Mountain Care after his administration concluded that financing it would require an 11.5% payroll tax and an income-based charge of up to 9.5%, warning that the “risk of economic shock” was too high.

California has reached the same conclusion in practice. Democrats have controlled the governor’s mansion since 2011 and have had supermajorities in both legislative chambers since 2018, yet they have failed to advance single-payer healthcare even to a floor vote.

If Medicare for All is such an obvious bargain, reducing costs while preserving quality without taxing the middle class, then why have Sanders’s Vermont and Rep. Ro Khanna’s (D-CA) California refused to enact it?

The reason is simple: Once Medicare for All stops being an empty promise and becomes a real plan with higher spending, lower provider pay, higher taxes, and rationed care, support for it, even in overwhelmingly Democratic states, collapses.

Self-identified socialist Democratic candidates are putting Medicare for All back on the ballot. Republicans should make sure voters understand that this means trillions in new federal spending, sweeping new taxes, the elimination of existing private coverage, and a government monopoly with the power to ration care. Democrats running this fall should answer for it.

news.title: From Booker-listed Marlon James to a memoir by Michael Douglas – the biggest books this autumn
news.text:
The Disappearers by Marlon JamesHamish Hamilton, 3 September
 After a detour into mythic fantasy, the author of the Booker-winning A Brief History of Seven Killings returns to Jamaica. This account of a brutal homophobic attack on a group of gay actors in 1980s Kingston has already been longlisted for this year’s prize.

The Bridge by Colm TóibínPicador, 3 September
 Twenty years on, this short novel is a sequel to Tóibín’s exquisite story A Long Winter, set around a family tragedy in the isolated Pyrenees. Now the building of a bridge brings modernity, possibility and threat to a father and son, in a spare chronicle of longing and grief.

The Golden Hours by Louisa YoungMantle, 3 September
 Young continues her aunt Elizabeth Jane Howard’s much-loved Cazalet Chronicles, bringing her story of a sprawling upper-middle-class English family into the swinging 60s.

Switzy by Emma ClineChatto & Windus, 10 September
 With dementia making him increasingly confused, David is on his way to a clinic in Zurich to end his life while he still has the capacity to make a choice. Longlisted for the Booker prize, this is a bravura portrait of a failing mind, told from the inside.

The Rouse by China MiévillePicador, 17 September
 A leading light of the New Weird, Miéville has been working on this stonking 1,000-page supernatural fantasy for two decades. Political intrigue, continent-hopping global conspiracy and uncanny mysteries unfold.

The Housekeeper by Rose TremainChatto & Windus, 17 September
 An origin story for Daphne du Maurier’s enduring bestseller Rebecca is told from the perspective of the novelist’s secret lover Danni, housekeeper in a Cornish mansion, who is outraged to find herself recast on the page as the malevolent Mrs Danvers.

Stations by Louise KennedyBloomsbury, 24 September
 The author of bestselling 2022 debut novel Trespasses, a Troubles-set love story recently adapted into a C4 drama starring Gillian Anderson, returns with a tale of friendship and loss. Róisín and Red meet in small-town Ireland in the 1980s and reconnect in a London squat, before Red is caught up in a cycle of poverty and addiction.

Doom Painting by AK BlakemoreGranta, 24 September
 One of our most exciting historical novelists takes on the peasants’ revolt, in a blow-by-blow account of unlikely leader Wat Tyler and the 16 days in 1381 that turned England upside down. With cinematic action and a relish for medieval vocabulary, it’s a punky successor to Hilary Mantel.

American Hagwon by Min Jin Lee
 4th Estate, 29 September
 The hagwon or cram school is a symbol of Korea’s stress on education. This new saga from the Pachinko author follows a middle-class family, their life in ruins after the 1997 Asian financial crisis, who move to Sydney and then California in search of a better future for their children.

Partita by Barbara KingsolverFaber, 6 October
 After the Pulitzer-winning Demon Copperhead, a retelling of David Copperfield set in Appalachia, Kingsolver returns with a quieter tale of midlife longing and regret. A gifted pianist, Livia used music to escape the sadness of her family life in rural Tennessee, but having married and resettled in her home town, an unexpected call from a former lover drags her back into the past.

Life Out of Order by Audrey NiffeneggerJonathan Cape, 13 October
 Set a quarter of a century on, this long-awaited sequel focuses on the daughter of the couple in The Time Traveler’s Wife. Alba has inherited her father’s extraordinary condition, jumping unpredictably across the decades, from a United States in turmoil to a dystopian future London. She’s torn between two lovers – one anchored in the present, and one a time traveller like herself.

Peck & Peck by Bonnie GarmusManilla, 13 October
 In the follow-up to global bestseller Lessons in Chemistry, it’s 1982 New York and young Batter Gray lands a job at the eponymous poetry periodical, run by feuding twin brothers. Expect charm, quirk and literary rabbit holes.

In One Brief Moment All Eternity by Elif ShafakViking, 15 October
 From the Booker and Women’s prize-shortlisted author, a study of French writer Gustave Flaubert refracted through the lives of the women around him, including his most iconic creation: Madame Bovary.

Music Against the Night by Yiyun Li
 4th Estate, 22 October
 Set at the end of the 18th century, against a background of global tumult, the Pulitzer winner’s historical epic is inspired by the lives of two musicians: Adelaide Percheron, born in French India, and the Irish John Field, the inventor of the nocturne, who will be brought together by love and talent.

Lessons in Harmony by Jonathan CoeViking, 12 November
 Music is in the air this autumn: Coe’s latest follows the friendship between French dandy Maurice Ravel and English traditionalist Ralph Vaughan Williams, exploring creativity and national identity against the encroaching shadow of the first world war.

Crime and thrillers

Sherlock Holmes, Miss Marple and George Smiley return

Autumn is back-to-school season for series authors, with William Boyd on the third of his cold war espionage novels starring travel writer Gabriel Dax. In Cold Sunset (Viking, 3 September) our reluctant spy is on his way to Russia, to tussle with the KGB. Richard Osman serves up number two in his We Solve Murders franchise: We Chase Shadows (Viking, 10 September) sees Steve, Amy and Rosie – retired cop, private security officer and bestselling crime author respectively – investigate after a body is found in the Italian hills. Five years on, Janice Hallett publishes a sequel to her hit am-dram debut The Appeal, as the Fairway Players’ new production of Agatha Christie leads to murder in The Silent Appeal (Viper, 3 September). The vigorous afterlife of the queen of crime continues elsewhere, with the first official new outing for Miss Marple, Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel by Lucy Foley (HarperCollins, 22 September). A varied cast list, death on the mountaintop and plenty of suspects are guaranteed.

Ian Rankin, known for his grumpy Edinburgh detective John Rebus, takes a new direction in The Heights (Orion, 8 October), a standalone thriller set in a luxurious central London high-rise. And there’s a return to the world of John le Carré’s Circus in the latest from his son Nick Harkaway: in The Taper Man (Viking, 5 November), George Smiley finds himself navigating the unlikely terrain of 1960s LA in search of a communist sleeper agent.

Finally, a festive treat: 10 new adventures for the world’s most famous detective in short story anthology Sherlock (Simon & Schuster, 5 November), with contributors including Sarah Perry, Joe Hill, Abir Mukherjee and Kate Mosse.

Swan Song: Diana, My Sister by Charles Spencer Penguin Michael Joseph, 22 September
 Thirty years after Princess Diana was killed in a car crash, her brother – whose euology at her funeral echoed around the world – tells the story of their upbringing and recounts the devastating week of her death.

The Castle by Jon Ronson Viking, 20 August
 A concerning late-night call from his teenage son marks the start of a strange journey into modern masculinity for the journalist and author of The Psychopath Test and So You’ve Been Publicly Shamed.

The Future Starts With Us by Gordon BrownSimon & Schuster, 1 September
 The former PM tries to join the dots between two seemingly disparate political phenomena: the erosion of the international rules-based order, exacerbated by war and climate breakdown, and the fragmentation of the tight-knit communities that keep us connected at a local level.

The Great Dictator: A Life of Barbara Cartland by Matthew Sweet Hodder & Stoughton, 10 September
 The queen of romance novels wrote a scarcely believable 723 of them during her career – with a little help from an amanuensis or two. Historian Sweet tells the extraordinary story of a woman born into an upper‑middle-class family fallen on hard times, who navigated scandal and opprobrium to become one of the bestselling writers of the 20th century.

Queens and Kings: An Unusually Personal History by Lucy Worsley Hodder & Stoughton, 3 September 
 The historian and chief curator of royal palaces brings a personal touch to some of British history’s pivotal moments, focusing on the places in which they unfolded, and in which Worsley herself has worked: Hampton Court, Kensington Palace and the Tower of London.

All the Wrong Moves by Anthony Scaramucci Bodley Head, 17 September
 Not many political figures are able to give Liz Truss a run for her money in the shortest-ever-tenure stakes, but Scaramucci, Trump’s press secretary for just 10 days, is one of them. Since then he’s reinvented himself as one of the administration’s sharpest critics. His first book is an attempt to chart how the US went from stable postwar consensus to today’s “shitshow politics”.

End Times Fascism by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor Allen Lane, 15 September
 Thinkers and activists Klein and Taylor have identified a distinctive strand of rightwing nihilism: the kind that seeks to reshape the world in its image, even as it devours the natural resources on which our survival depends (certain tech barons and authoritarian leaders may feel particularly seen). Here they offer both a diagnosis and a plan for resistance.

Profits, Prophets, Coaches and Kings: (When) Do Leaders Make a Difference? by Jared Diamond Mariner, 22 September
 The author of Guns, Germs and Steel, known for his analyses of the grand, impersonal forces that shape human destiny, returns with a timely book on the role of prominent individuals. What difference does a sports coach, a CEO or an erratic president really make to the fortunes of teams, companies and global civilisation?

An Unexpected Life: A Memoir by Gloria Steinem Ebury, 22 September
 A totemic figure in American feminism, Steinem sought to carry the momentum of the civil rights era into what became known as the women’s liberation movement. Here she writes about her childhood and political awakening, and reflects from the present moment on nearly 60 years of activism.

Hawking: His Life and Work by Graham FarmeloJohn Murray, 24 September
 In the first authorised biography of Stephen Hawking, Farmelo paints an intimate portrait of the acclaimed physicist based on unique access to his diaries and letters, as well as interviews with family and close associates.

The American Way of Killing: The Invention of an Epidemic by Malcolm GladwellAbacus, 29 September
 The author of The Tipping Point asks why the United States has ended up being so much more violent than comparable countries around the world. From a Chicago ER to a 17th-century court case, he explores stories that may hold the key to what he describes as “the most pressing of all American social problems”.

Blockers: Rebels in the Deep State by Michael Lewis Allen Lane, 6 October
 Lewis’s pacy, high-stakes nonfiction has been drawing readers since 1989’s Liar’s Poker, an account of his time on Wall Street in the 1980s. Here he deploys his powers of narration to tell the story of how the US Department of Government Efficiency (Doge) sought to dismantle the state – though his real subject is the principled civil servants who stood in the way of Elon Musk’s campaign of vandalism.

Requiem for Gaza by Joe Sacco and Chris Hedges Jonathan Cape, 8 October 
 The master of graphic reportage and author of Palestine teams up with veteran war correspondent Hedges to document the devastating Israeli war on Gaza and its human impact. Interviewing 29 displaced Palestinian families, Sacco and Hedges tell stories of death, destruction and resilience.

The Perilous Fight by Colin KaepernickGrand Central Publishing, 8 October
 The NFL quarterback made history in 2016 when he knelt for the US national anthem, rather than standing. Since that time, “taking the knee” has become an emblem of the fight for racial justice, in the US and beyond. In his memoir, Kaepernick traces the relationships and experiences that culminated in a pivotal sporting and political moment.

Promise Me, America by Joe BidenJohn Murray, 17 November
 A year on from 107 Days, in which former vice-president Kamala Harris detailed her boss’s failure to get out of the way, Joe Biden tells his side of the story in a book which promises to reveal “the deeply agonising calculation behind his decision … to step aside from the presidential race”.

Pay Attention by Laura KuenssbergCorsair, 5 November 
 The former BBC political editor’s first book reflects on 20 years of upheaval in British politics, and what the broadcaster perceives as being at the root of it all: a failure by the political class to really listen to what people have actually been saying.

Holding Lightning: The Life, Loves and Art of Whitney Houston by Emily LordiWhite Rabbit, 1 October
 English professor Lordi treats the career of one of pop’s greatest stars with the seriousness it deserves, but with emotional intelligence too, tracing the arc of Houston’s life from global success to personal tragedy.

From Hollywood hijinks to political scandal – life stories to look out for

It’s another bumper autumn for Hollywood stars with plenty of tales to tell – though this year skews male. Michael Douglas’s One Helluva Ride (Headline, 6 October) includes details of “affairs with some of the most celebrated actresses in Hollywood” and the “serious drug addiction that threatened to destroy his first marriage and career”. If you’re still in the mood for testosterone-laced hijinks after that, there’s Sylvester Stallone’s The Steps (Seven Dials, 29 September), which charts the Rocky star’s 1970s journey from homelessness to the Oscars. For a more multilayered take on acting and fame, try Fictional Selves by Kyle MacLachlan (Century, 29 September), whose talent in picking idiosyncratic roles such as such as Agent Cooper in Twin Peaks has earned him a cult following. And then there’s screen icon Dustin Hoffman, whose first memoir Look at Me (Gallery, 10 November), published as he prepares to enter his 10th decade, covers the pressures of being dubbed the “voice of a generation” after The Graduate, and his many acting roles since that extraordinary breakthrough. It would make a neat pairing with Watergate reporter Bob Woodward’s memoir Secrets (Simon & Schuster, 24 November): that era-defining scoop was dramatised in All the President’s Men, with Hoffman playing Woodward’s partner, Carl Bernstein.

On the other side of the Atlantic, Judi Dench reminisces about a 70-year career in Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It? (Michael Joseph, 22 October). In Vigilauntie (W&N, 3 September) actor and co-creator of the groundbreaking sketch show Goodness Gracious Me, Meera Syal, writes about family, frustration and making it as an Asian woman on TV, while another veteran of the small screen, Russell T Davies, charts a writing career that has spanned Coronation Street and Doctor Who in The Queerest of Folk (Bantam, 8 October). Everyone’s favourite communist standup Alexei Sayle gets political in How I’ve Tried to Change the World (W&N, 3 September), a memoir of protest through the decades, while actual politician and scourge of the BNP in her Barking constituency, Margaret Hodge, shares the lessons of a life on the frontlines in Battle Axe (William Collins, 10 September).
news.summary:
Midlife meditations from Barbara Kingsolver; musical portraits by Jonathan Coe and Yiyun Li; plus memoirs from Dustin Hoffman and Judi Dench – all among the coming season’s highlights

news.title: On This Day, Aug. 22: IRA founder Michael Collins assassinated
news.text:
Aug. 22 (UPI) -- On this date in history:

In 1851, the U.S.-built schooner America outran a fleet of Britain's finest ships around England's Isle of Wight in an international race that became known as the America's Cup.

In 1881, American humanitarians Clara Barton and Adolphus Solomons founded the National Red Cross.

In 1922, Michael Collins, a founder of the Irish Republican Army and a key figure in Ireland's independence movement, was assassinated by political opponents.

In 1968, Pope Paul VI arrived in Colombia, becoming the first pontiff to visit South America.

In 1986, Kerr-McGee Corp. agreed to pay the estate of nuclear industry worker Karen Silkwood more than $1 million, ending a 10-year legal battle waged by her family over her exposure to radioactive materials at the company's Oklahoma plant.

In 2004, two masked robbers stole Edvard Munch's The Scream and another painting from the Munch Museum in Oslo, Norway. They were found about two years later and put back on display in 2008. The Scream had been stolen once before, 10 years earlier, but was recovered within three months.

In 2005, the last Jewish settlers moved peacefully out of the Gaza Strip after carrying Torah scrolls down the main street of Netzarim, last of 21 settlements to be evacuated.

In 2006, Pulkovo Airlines Flight 612 crashed near the Russian border in Ukraine, killing 171 people.

In 2011, the Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. National Memorial in Washington opened to the public. The $120 million memorial, 25 years in the making, is on a four-acre site on the National Mall.

In 2017, India's Supreme Court declared the "instant divorce" practice among the nation's Muslim population to be unconstitutional.

In 2021, Vice President Kamala Harris visited Singapore, her first visit to Asia as VP, to discuss issues of climate change, the COVID-19 pandemic and supply chain concerns with Singapore Prime Minister Lee Shien Loong.
news.summary: On Aug. 22, 1922, Michael Collins, a founder of the Irish Republican Army and a key figure in Ireland's independence movement, was assassinated.

news.title: How 35-year-old Natalie Harp Became Donald Trump's Favorite Assistant
news.text:
In recent years, few people in US President Donald Trump's entourage have appeared beside him as frequently as his assistant, 35-year-old Natalie Harp, reports the BBC.

Natalie Harp is one of Trump's long-standing and most loyal aides.

This week, she once again found herself in the spotlight due to statements made by Trump's opponent, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia. The politician unleashed a new wave of criticism on Trump and mentioned Natalie Harp in his speech, which widely circulated on social media.

Criticizing the president, Ossoff stated:

“He [Trump] doesn’t want to do his job. He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on what appears to be their entirely defenseless flying palace, gifted by the Emir of Qatar.”

 The senator was referring to the new presidential aircraft Air Force One ("Aircraft One"), as well as journalists' reports that Harp likely flew with Trump on a secret flight from Turkey after the NATO summit. 

Earlier, the American press reported that Trump, upon departing from Ankara in early July, used an in-flight catering van to discreetly transfer from "Aircraft One" to "Aircraft Two." The secret flight, as reported by the media, was linked to an alleged threat from Iran.

Cancer and an Unusual Path to the White House

Natalie Harp was born in California to a Christian family with conservative views. Her path to the White House can be described as atypical.

 She became known for crediting Trump with saving her life. 

During his first term, Trump pushed for the passage of the Right to Try Act, which gave patients broader access to experimental treatments. Harp was then able to use this opportunity to receive treatment for bone cancer using experimental methods, as traditional chemotherapy had not yielded positive results in her case.

“When the available chemotherapy didn't work, nobody wanted to take me for clinical trials […] They didn't give me the right to try experimental treatments, Mr. President. You did, and without you, I would have died waiting for their permission,” she said at the 2020 Republican National Convention.

 After the event, Trump said that Natalie Harp, with her appearance, "lit up the television screen like few" he had ever seen. 

Natalie Harp, who frequently spoke about her treatment experience and expressed gratitude to Trump, was quickly recognized within the MAGA ("Make America Great Again") wing of the Republican Party.

Soon after, she joined the campaign's advisory board during Trump's 2020 election campaign.

"Trump's Biggest Supporter"

After Trump's defeat in the 2020 election, Harp became a host on the right-wing conservative cable news channel One America News Network (OAN).

There, she became known as a staunch defender of Donald Trump, also claiming that he had allegedly won the 2020 election.

She left the TV channel in 2022 to join Trump's next presidential campaign.

Most information regarding Trump's relationship with Harp comes from anonymous sources, mentioned in books by journalists such as Maggie Haberman, Jonathan Swan, or Michael Wolff. Almost nothing is known about Natalie Harp's personal life.

Her brother, Preston Harp, explained his sister's unusual devotion to Trump in a CNN interview by saying that the current president embodies everything their mother taught them to respect in life.

“That’s why I think, honestly, her fascination with Trump comes from there,” Preston Harp said.

He added that Harp had been obsessed with the idea of working in the White House since she was young and had written letters to previous presidents, including George W. Bush during the Iraq War.

In a CNN interview, Harp's brother said that her “dream finally came true” when she got into the White House, and that his sister was “Trump’s biggest supporter, so he probably likes her.”

 “She’s beautiful, she has a good character. She thinks he saved her life, so a person for whom such gratitude is felt must feel very good about it,” he said. 

Harp's official position at the White House is Executive Assistant to the President, a role not typically high-level, involving managing logistics, scheduling, and communication flow.

However, it appears Harp has given this role new meaning, and her authority is significantly higher than that of her predecessors, such as Madeleine Westerhout in Trump's first administration.

What Influence Does Natalie Harp Have on Trump?

When CNN reporter Kristen Holmes asked Trump this week about Ossoff’s comments, the US president lashed out at her with criticism. “You’re being very disrespectful… Fake news, you’re fake news […] You’re a fake journalist and you report fake news,” Trump reacted to the reporter’s question.

The White House later published a video recording of Trump’s conversation with the journalist on its official X page, accusing her of using a “cheap” and crude tactic in her work.

“One day your children will learn about your disgusting and inhumane question. They will be uncomfortable and ashamed to see a parent display such heartlessness,” another post addressed to Holmes stated.

Trump's aide, Natalie Harp, is almost inseparable from President Donald Trump during his second term.

 Reporters at the White House often see her just steps away from Trump in the Oval Office or aboard Air Force One during many of his domestic and international trips. 

“She’s always there. Literally always,” a source close to the White House told the BBC.

Among those close to the White House and press representatives, she is often called a "living printer," as she is frequently seen with a portable printer, which she needs to print articles and social media posts for Trump on paper — because he prefers to read publications on paper.

This means that Harp likely has significant opportunities to control exactly what information and messages Trump receives, notes another source familiar with White House operations.

Other anonymous sources described her to American media as the president's "gatekeeper" and "favorite toy."

Harp also acts as a kind of social media secretary for Trump: she posts messages on his Truth Social account on his behalf.

In one video that widely circulated on social media after Ossoff’s comments, Harp is captured typing text for social media at Trump’s dictation, as he watches Kamala Harris’s 2024 speech.

Amid recent attention on Harp, the White House stated that she is a “trusted and valuable” member of the team, though Trump himself has rarely spoken about her on camera.

Ossoff was one of many Trump critics who noted that Harp was reportedly on board the plane on which the president departed from Turkey after the US allegedly received intelligence about a threat from Iran.

 When journalist Maggie Haberman, who has written extensively and continues to write about Trump's presidency, was asked during an interview why Trump took Harp with him on "Aircraft Two" when departing from Turkey on a secret flight, she replied: "Because for him, if one can put it this way, she's like a pacifier, like a favorite warm blanket, a favorite toy — in short, something that creates a feeling of comfort and peace."
Haberman and Jonathan Swan reported in a 2024 New York Times publication that Harp allegedly wrote in a letter to Trump: "You are everything that matters to me."

news.title: Trump says he would be happy if allowed to run for third presidential term
news.text:
WASHINGTON, August 22. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump said he would be happy if the country's laws were changed to allow him to run for a third term as head of state.

"We have rules and regulation that says you're not allowed to run. If they'd like to change that, be very happy," Trump told supporters in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina.

By law, Trump's second term as president is scheduled to end in January 2029. The 22nd Amendment to the US Constitution, adopted in 1951, limits a president to two terms in office. However, the current American leader has repeatedly raised the possibility of seeking reelection to a third term.

Trump won the presidency for a second time in November 2024, defeating Democratic candidate Kamala Harris. He previously served his first term from 2017 to 2021.
news.summary: Donald Trump won the presidency for a second time in November 2024, defeating Democratic candidate Kamala Harris
news.author: Tass

news.title: US VP Vance campaigns in hometown with eye on 2028
news.text:
US vice-president JD Vance said the Trump administration is 'making progress' on issues including 'the affordability question' amid anger over rising prices. (EPA Images pic)
MIDDLETOWN: US vice-president JD Vance returned to his hometown Friday to campaign for Republicans in November's crucial midterm elections - and test his own hopes of succeeding Donald Trump in 2028.
Vance gave a speech at the steel plant where his grandfather worked for 40 years in Middletown, Ohio, the blue-collar town which featured in his bestselling 2016 memoir "Hillbilly Elegy".
The book recounted an impoverished upbringing in the neglected rust belt that spawned Trump's "Make America Great Again" movement, which Vance needs to woo if he runs for the White House in two years.
But Vance is also seeking to boost Republican candidates ahead of the midterms, amid fears that Trump's unpopularity could cause the party to lose control of Congress.
Trump's approval rating has fallen to 33 percent, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted last week, the lowest of his current term.
Vance took a subtly centrist tone in his speech, evoking his blue-collar upbringing while avoiding much of the harsh rhetoric that has made Trump so divisive.
"I remember my papaw... coming to this very place to work for nearly 40 years as a welder," Vance said.
The isolationist vice-president, who has privately opposed Trump's Iran war, said his grandfather had "very simple" expectations including that "America never be asked to be the policeman of the world".
Vance added that the Trump administration was "making progress" on issues including "the affordability question". Voters have voiced anger over rising prices, which his boss has dismissed as a hoax launched by rival Democrats.
But the 42-year-old also had harsh words for the opposition on subjects including immigration and so-called "woke" politics.
Urging Republicans to vote in November, he said: "Get out there and fight for yourself by telling the far-left radicals who have taken over the Democratic Party: 'This is not your country. It's our country, and we're going to fight for it.'"
The race to succeed Trump in 2028 - assuming he does not try for a constitutionally barred third term - is set to begin in earnest after the midterms.
Vance has declined to formally confirm that he will run but has been clearly positioning himself as the heir to Trump's MAGA movement, albeit without the rough edges.
But many in the Republican party are also looking at US secretary of state Marco Rubio as a contender.
Rubio has said he will not run if Vance does, but a poll by Emerson College and The Hill released this week found that Rubio outperformed Vance in all but one of five match-ups against leading Democratic contenders.
The Democrats meanwhile face their own struggles as they seek to rebuild from Trump's 2024 defeat of then-vice-president Kamala Harris.
The far-left wing of the Democratic Party has scored a series of primary wins in recent months, even as centrists seek to distance themselves from socialist-style proposals like universal health care.
news.summary: JD Vance is also seeking to boost Republican candidates ahead of November's midterm elections amid fears the party could lose control of Congress.
news.author: AFP

news.title: Whatley Within Striking Distance of Defeating Roy Cooper in North Carolina
news.text: Republican Michael Whatley is within striking distance of former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper in the race for North Carolina’s open U.S. Senate seat, according to a new High Point University poll released Friday. The race is for the seat currently held by Republican Senator Thom Tillis, who is not seeking reelection. Cooper, who served as North Carolina governor from 2017 through 2024, is seeking a return to elected office, while Whatley is the former chairman of the Republican National Committee (RNC) and the North Carolina Republican Party. Jeff Allen, Cooper for North Carolina campaign manager, told Newsweek via email on Friday when asked about the new poll, "Roy Cooper has spent his career putting North Carolinians first, while Washington, D.C., insider Michael Whatley spent his delivering for billionaires and special interests at the expense of the middle class. A Democrat has not won statewide federal office in North Carolina in nearly two decades and we know this race will be very close, which is why we’re building a campaign to earn every vote and make sure North Carolinians know that Roy Cooper will fight for them in the Senate." Newsweek also reached out to Whatley's campaign via email on Friday for comment. Why It Matters Republicans in the Senate hold a 53-45 majority—excluding independent Senators Bernie Sanders and Angus King, who caucus with Democrats—and Democrats view flipping the seat as a potential pathway to taking control of the upper chamber. Midterm elections are also commonly seen as a measure of public approval for the current president too, and the president's party has traditionally lost seats during these elections. Trump has backed Whatley in the race, adding another layer of potential intensity. What To Know The contest is viewed as one of the key Senate races of the 2026 midterms, with the outcome potentially affecting control of the chamber. The Cook Political Report has the race slated as Lean Democrat. The poll showed that among likely voters, Cooper leads Whatley 50 percent to 45 percent, a 5-point advantage that falls within the poll’s 5.2-percentage-point credibility interval. The poll shows that 3 percent are unsure or would not vote and 3 percent would pick someone else or another party. The survey of 800 self-identified registered voters, including 660 likely voters, was conducted August 3-12. The poll marks a closer contest than some recent surveys have suggested. Among all self-identified registered voters, Cooper leads Whatley 48 percent to 41 percent, with 8 percent unsure or saying they would not vote and 4 percent saying they would pick someone else or another party. The HPU poll gives that group a 4.3-percentage-point credibility interval. Grant Reeher, professor of political science at Syracuse University, told Newsweek via email on Friday in part, "One has to be careful about slicing the results too thin. It was also an online poll, as I understand it. I’d be wary of investing too much meaning in a couple point shift from previous polls when the margin of error is 5 points." "But having said all that," Reeher added, "a smallish shift is not surprising, given the recent unpopularity of the Iran War, and persistent inflation and interest rate concerns. It’s still anyone’s race, even though I agree with Cook that it looks like it’s leaning toward the Dems. And Cooper may not have as much of the negativity associated with the Democratic brand as some other candidates." D. Stephen Voss, political science professor at the University of Kentucky, also told Newsweek via email on Friday: "The tightening of the North Carolina race makes sense because of the name-recognition advantage Roy Cooper enjoyed going into the contest. Likely voters knew him and many knew they were ready to support him. Fewer voters knew Michael Whatley, reporting neither a favorable nor an unfavorable opinion of him. "It makes sense that as the race gained more attention, the sort of people who typically vote Republican would be returning to the fold, leaving fewer likely voters still unsure of what they'll do. That's the educational function that election season performs. Once Whatley finishes picking up the voters who always should have been his, though, persuading the remainder will become just as hard for him as it is for Cooper," Voss concluded. The HPU poll points to a challenging political environment for Republicans in the state. Among likely voters, 59 percent say the country is on the wrong track, compared with 36 percent who say it is headed in the right direction. Trump’s approval rating stands at 42 percent, with 54 percent disapproving, while 48 percent of likely voters say North Carolina itself was on the wrong track. Those broader numbers could give Cooper an advantage, but Whatley’s five-point deficit among likely voters is close enough that the race remains competitive with less than three months until Election Day. Trump won the swing state in the 2024 presidential election versus former Vice President Kamala Harris by 3.3 percent. What Other Polls Show Other recent polling has generally shown Cooper with a larger advantage. An Elon University poll released earlier this month found Cooper ahead of Whatley 53 percent to 42 percent among likely voters. The poll surveyed 800 North Carolina adults from July 23 to July 31, 2026, and has a margin of error of 5.6 percent for likely voters. A Carolina Journal Poll shows Cooper leading with 51.5 percent to Whatley's 39 percent. The survey, conducted by Harper Polling, was from August 9 to August 10, 2026, and has a margin of error of 4 percent. What's Next for Whatley and Cooper Neither campaign has published a public calendar of events for the upcoming week; however, here's what's expected: Both campaigns appear to be ramping up in-person events as the November 3 election approaches and recent polling continues to show a competitive race. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Trump has backed Whatley in the race, adding another layer of potential intensity.
news.author: Anna Commander

news.title: California’s Home of Chicken and Waffles suddenly shuts down after 20-year run
news.text:
Get clucked, the kitchen is closing.

After a decades-long run dishing up chicken and waffles, an Oakland staple is closing its doors for good. Home of Chicken and Waffles announced the closure on its website telling guests its last day to scarf down a plate will be on August 31.

“Thank you for all the years of love and friendship!” The spot wrote.

The closing brings the end of a 23-year long era, as founder Derreck Johnson first opened the joint back in 2004 at its first location on Embarcadero West. It later moved to its current spot on Fourth Street in 2024.

The southern staple was not only known for its soul food but its community outreach as it employed formerly incarcerated workers. The spot also drew high-profile customers like Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris.

Johnson told SF Gate he is “Very happy and excited about [closing].” After 23 years, I want out of the restaurant business. I’m just ready to move on.” 

The restaurant did not give a specific reason behind the closure but Johnson told multiple outlets that he is looking forward to the next chapter and will announce more details about the future in the coming months.

Customers flooded to social media after the announcement with lifelong eaters mourning. 

“Awwww Derrick’s presence and food has been a legendary comfort to so many folks here! Wishing my frat brother much success and love for what comes next!” One wrote on Instagram. 

Download The California Post App, follow us on social, and subscribe to our newsletters 

On remembering what Johnson did for the community, one customer commented, “job well done, you’ve helped sooooooo many of us & helped us become who we are today thank you so much for the opportunity & the love you. Poured into us all we were family & many of us are still connected looking forward to what’s to come ahead.”

Another Bay Area favorite is closed down after nearly 15 years. Pucquio, a Peruvian restaurant in Rockridge, served up its last dish back in July.

The spot announced the shutter on Instagram, stunning customers. 

“A chapter is closing, but the memories we’ve shared will last forever. Thank you for every visit, every celebration, and for allowing us to share the flavors of Peru with you. It has been an honor to be part of your story,” the Oakland spot said.

news.title: Trump underwater in 47 states and DC, new projection finds
news.text:
Amid President Donald Trump’s record-low approval ratings nationally, a new YouGov/Economist projection shows the president's net job approval is negative in all but three states.

According to The Economist and YouGov, more people disapprove than approve of Trump’s job performance in 47 out of 50 states and in the District of Columbia. The three states where the majority of respondents still approve of the president are Wyoming (+14), Idaho (+9), and West Virginia (+6). 

All three went for Trump in the 2016, 2020, and 2020 presidential elections.

The lowest net job approval rating for Trump was in D.C. (-83). The two states that disapprove of the president's job the most are Maryland and Vermont, both at -50. The three are all historically Democratic strongholds that voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024.

The White House did not immediately respond to USA TODAY’s request for comment on Friday, Aug. 21.

See map of Trump’s net approval

A historic run

Trump’s negative net approval in most states in the country comes as the president continues to see record-low approval numbers in nationwide polling.

In a new Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Aug. 17, only one in three Americans said they approved of Trump’s job performance, the lowest approval rating the president has seen in Reuters/Ipsos tracking since his return to the White House in 2025.

Trump’s bad polling numbers come as an overwhelming majority of Americans said they were concerned that the war against Iran would continue for an extended period.

In the Aug. 17 poll, 80% of Americans, including 87% of Democrats and 71% of Republicans, believed the U.S. involvement with Iran would continue for an “extended period of time.”

What do polling averages show?

While individual polls vary, major polling averages continue to show Trump in negative territory overall:

RealClearPolitics (Aug. 21): 39.5% approve, 57.2% disapproveNew York Times (Aug. 21): 37% approve, 59% disapproveSilver Bulletin (Aug. 21): 38.2% approve, 57.9% disapprove

USA TODAY’s Kinsey Crowley contributed to this report.
