news.title: Ariana Grande calls out Donald Trump after her music appears in anti-trans TikTok
news.text: Ariana Grande has delivered a sharp rebuke to Donald Trump after his team featured her music in an anti-trans TikTok video . A clip uploaded to TikTok by Team Trump on Thursday showed the president striding towards the stage at a political rally. Text overlaying the footage declared: "Me and my truth we sit in silence... men can't have babies and should never compete in women's sports." Team Trump accompanied the post with the caption: "This decision shouldn't be controversial! #trump #arianagrande #maga." The video originally included Grande's 2024 hit We Can't Be Friends (Wait for Your Love), though the audio has now been removed. Grande hit back in the comments, marking yet another instance where she's been forced to challenge Trump's unauthorised use of her work. In her August 20 response, Grande wrote: "Never use my music again. Also, your truth is false", reports the Mirror US . This is the second time Grande has confronted Trump over music usage. Previously in June, the 33 year old pop sensation warned Trump against incorporating her song in an anti-ICE TikTok. That row began when the White House used her 2024 track Bye in a TikTok video showing ICE agents making arrests. The clip depicted ICE officers handcuffing several individuals. The clip was captioned: "Bye-bye. President Trump has delivered the most secure border in history." Grande responded sharply, writing: "Please do not ever use my music in relation to this barbaric, inhumane, heinous nonsense. F- ICE." Both her comment and the track have since been deleted from the TikTok post. While Grande's remark disappeared from the TikTok footage, a spokesperson for the pop star verified to Billboard that it was authentically Grande who left the comment and noted it had vanished "for some reason." Grande also took aim at the Trump administration during the 2026 Golden Globe Awards ceremony, where the Wicked star sported an ICE Out pin. In September 2025, Grande reshared an Instagram message condemning Trump regarding ICE operations and anti-trans language. The initial post was penned by activist Matt Bernstein and stated: "I want to check in with trump voters. I have one very genuine question. It's been 250 days. now that immigrants have been violently torn from their families and communities have been destroyed. "Now that trans people have been blamed for virtually everything and live in fear, now that free speech is on the brink of collapse for us all - has your life gotten better?" Throughout the 2024 presidential race, Grande backed Democratic contender Kamala Harris. She had previously taken to the stage for Barack Obama and Michelle Obama at the 2014 In Performance at the White House: Women of Soul occasion.
news.summary: Ariana Grande has issued a warning to Donald Trump after his team used her music in an anti-trans TikTok video, with the singer telling the president to "never use my music again"

news.title: On Michael Cohen’s Radio Show, Donald Trump Is Back to Being the “Boss”
news.text:
“The American people have spoken and re-elected Donald Trump,” Cohen wrote in an email. “Accordingly, I believe we must all acknowledge and respect the office of the Presidency and dismiss the case forthwith.”
Shocking as this development was, in retrospect, it may have been a preview of the reconciliation to come. Ever since Trump was reelected and guaranteed a return to the kind of power to which Cohen, by his own account in his memoirs and courtroom testimony, has long been drawn, the two men who had previously described one another as “fraud” and “rat” have been inching towards a full-fledged reunion: first, Cohen said earlier this year that he had “felt compelled and coerced to deliver what [prosecutors] were seeking.” Then he met with Trump at Mar-a-Lago and his Bedminster golf club. Cohen had orchestrated the payment to Stormy Daniels that in part sent him to prison in 2019, testifying in 2024 that he had done so at Trump’s direction. But on Thursday night, a month into his new role as a host on the Trump-aligned billionaire John Catsimatidis’s New York radio station, his tenor was ecstatic as he introduced his biggest guest to date.
“Tonight,” Cohen said, “you are tuning into something that people thought that they would never live to see.”
“Hello, Michael,” Trump said as he called in.
Such was Cohen’s early admiration for Trump that he bought two apartments at Trump World Tower in the 2000s. They first connected after Trump appreciated Cohen’s ferocious approach in a dispute with the building’s condo board, and the Long Island-bred lawyer has evinced a flair for melodrama at every turn in their roller-coaster relationship since, releasing books titled Disloyal and Revenge after emerging from prison in 2020. He was in rare form this week as he geared up for the interview with his old boss, explaining to listeners that “forgiveness does not mean amnesia” or “that the pain was fake or that I have forgotten a single second of what transpired.”
“Can loyalty survive the ultimate fallout?” Cohen went on, seeming to stretch the limits of his poetic capacities. “Can friendship exist after deep betrayal? Can two people who stood together at the summit and then tore each other apart in the valley actually find common ground again?”
To be sure, Cohen may have an ulterior motive for this dizzying rapprochement. He told CNN on Thursday that he had submitted a pardon application to the White House and planned to follow up the next day; Trump is currently appealing his felony conviction related to the infamous hush-money payment. “I respect the fact that you recanted everything you said,” Trump told Cohen on the air. “And that’s a big thing that you did.” (While it’s not clear what Cohen has privately said to Trump, he has not retracted the testimony he gave under oath.)
With that out of the way, Trump began to ramble: about Iran, about Venezuela, about how “the rallies are potentially bigger than ever,” about how Kamala Harris “knew less about the border than a child would know.” Cohen barely got a word in, but he slipped into reminiscence easily: “Boss, you remember when I was by your side?” During the decade-long period when Cohen played Trump’s antagonist in a national psychodrama, he looked agitated and haggard, but now, he sounded as if he had stepped back into a prior state of exhilarated comfort that had never quite worn off. In Disloyal, Cohen asks himself about the source of his “starstruck, moth-to-the-flame compulsion to insinuate [himself] with a man so transparently problematic in myriad ways.”
The answer, he wrote, “included something deeper than the obvious lures of money and power, though those were crucial factors. It was physical, emotional, not quite spiritual, but a deep longing and need that Trump filled for me. Around Trump I felt excited, alive, like he possessed the urgent and only truth, the chance for my salvation and success in life.”
news.summary: After a long, vicious feud that ricocheted across the national press and a Manhattan courtroom, the president and his former fixer reunited this week on Cohen’s radio show for an interview that immediately slipped into a cozy rapport of kindred spirits.

news.title: GOP is finally running out of people to blame
news.text:
Now that Donald Trump no longer has a White House press secretary with a ready cherubic smile and a ton of snark, we can all see that the paint is peeling off his delusional presidency. 

I’m not just talking about the Reflecting Pool.

Republicans like Rep. Byron Donalds, now the GOP nominee to succeed Ron DeSantis as governor of Florida, has habitually and enthusiastically repeated and amplified Trump’s whims and still claims with a straight face — as he did on Fox News this week — that Democratic policy and the actions of Joe Biden and Kamala Harris are responsible for the horror under which we currently live. Never mind the fact the Democrats currently hold no power in Washington and can’t implement any policies of any kind.

At least Republicans are finally, if obliquely, admitting that things aren’t so good in the country. Trump, however, isn’t ready to concede that. According to him, America would have burst into flames and melted into the bedrock mantle if he hadn’t come to town. Now? We hear many in and out of government saying that his presence ensures the outcome he predicted the Democrats would visit upon us all. 

Like I say, the paint is peeling. 

Time for this commercial break. On Wednesday, Trump was seen on the South Lawn praising a brand of fertilizer made by a company that, as he noted, had given him a sizable campaign contribution. Trump says it’s great stuff. Hey, they paid. He played. Very often, he is exactly as transparent as he claims to be. At the end of this live commercial he said that this fertilizer made for “happy grass.” He sounded like he’d been smoking some of that stuff. 

On the one hand, this is incredible corruption, but if you’re a CEO, having the president push your product directly in front of the White House isn’t a bad thing. You can’t blame business for doing what business does. You can blame the rest of us for not stopping it before it got this bad.

Yep, the paint is peeling.

To overcome the absence of departed pep secretary Karoline Leavitt, Byron Donalds and the rest of Trump’s puppets have been dancing long and hard lately. Speaker of the House Mike Johnson told reporters the economy had taken off and was on its way into the stratosphere until we experienced this little detour “called Iran.” You could say he unwittingly justified every American’s anger over a pointless, useless war that is making all our lives more difficult and more expensive. He was trying to back up his leader, but accidentally threw him to the wolves. But was it really accidental? 

The key point here is that the GOP has been in charge in D.C. for more than a year and a half. Republicans control the Senate, the House, the Supreme Court and the presidency. They vowed they’d fix the economy and have only moved the needle backward. Everyone who pays rent, utilities and grocery bills and worries about what they’ll do if they have to face a sudden health crisis knows it.

Republicans are screaming about socialism ruining the country while those so-called socialists are pushing free healthcare. Who do you think the American public will listen to? The GOP’s pitch was, roughly speaking, that they could use extreme methods to take care of the cleanup on aisle seven. They have obviously failed. Now other folks are making the same claim from the opposite side of the court. I remain skeptical that any political party in this country can affect real and lasting positive change. They’re too busy demonizing each other, with Trump as lead demon who, along with other minor imps, feed on the filthy lucre of oligarchs and billionaires.

Even if Trump and his lesser demons, in their bacchanalian zeal, were right in pinning blame for how the country got the way it is on Biden and the Democrats — and I’m not saying they are — their self-incriminating statements amount to admitting that they can’t handle the problem either. If you got elected to fix the system and nearly two years later everything is much worse, then it’s time to hire a new plumber — and not the Richard Nixon type.

Making a sale to the electorate as a Republican this year is a difficult task indeed. Even the disorganized Democrats might be able to crawl over that low bar. We can’t say a GOP victory is impossible, but it seems conditional on a variety of narrowing possibilities, especially considering the accused criminals, domestic abusers and otherwise morally bankrupt candidates they are offering us. Then there are the Democrats. All the Republicans can do is accuse the party that’s out of power of somehow wielding the power, and doing so as part of a sinister communist conspiracy. These midterms promise to be fun: the old and befuddled far right versus the young and arrogant far left, vying for attention and a chance to feed at the public trough.

Even corrupt public servants deserve a second chance. Sure, some of them should have to work in soup kitchens for a decade to earn that second chance — you know, in addition to whatever prison time they serve. After all, we want good people. 

But no one who’s been convicted of 34 felonies should get another chance. If he never goes to prison, he should be forced to work the rest of his natural life handing out free meals in a soup kitchen in an impoverished county in the Deep South, with weekends spent answering phones on the substance abuse hotline. 

Paint peeling. Hear it?

Remember Michael Cohen? He was the former Trump “fixer” who testified against his ex-boss in the New York criminal case. He also testified in a highly publicized congressional hearing on Feb. 27, 2019, telling the House Oversight Committee that Trump was a “racist,” a “con man” and a “cheat.”

On his podcast, Cohen he has often referred to Trump with a scatological insult (“VonS***zInPantz”), which even entered the official court transcript during the 2024 hush-money trial when Trump’s defense attorney brought it up.

But the paint is peeling, and Cohen recently got a chance to interview Trump for his podcast. Some liberals who have welcomed Cohen’s criticisms of Trump are now calling him a weasel, a sell-out and worse, turning the scatological nickname back at him. Hey, the American public can be crude and cruel. Those two guys definitely know about that.

For the documentary “The First 100 Days,” I asked Cohen in January 2025 what he might ask Trump if he got the chance to talk to him. Cohen said he believed he was owed an explanation.

Many journalists would love to get the opportunity to interview Trump one-on-one, and might pursue more ambitious lines of questioning. The fact that Trump gave an interview to someone who has publicly called him a racist, a con man and a cheat, and who has suggested that the president is incontinent, says a lot about both men. Hey, it should give us hope. It sounds like Trump is desperate to tell his story to literally anyone.

Few, perhaps, would have employed the same tactics Cohen used. But the folks at Breitbart, News Nation and similar outlets who preface their briefing-room questions by referencing “mainstream media” can only wish they were as successful as Cohen in getting Trump on their show.

Those who do interview Trump should treat him no differently than we used to treat the accused criminals we interviewed on “America’s Most Wanted.” That’s why I’ll never interview him while he’s president. 

So how did Cohen’s interview with Trump turn out? On Thursday we got a preview. It sounded a lot like Trump’s standard stump speech. He began by saying the country is doing well and Cohen responding, “Thanks to you, Mr. President.” Both said they were victims of a “weaponized” Department of Justice. Later on, Cohen volunteered to stage a presidential press conference and played “Reunited” by Peaches & Herb. People are too busy searching for things “to be enraged about,” he said. Cohen ended the 20-minute preview by saying that he’s putting the past behind him and that the $40 trillion national debt is a huge problem. Then he played “Why Can’t We Be Friends?” by War. 

Would it surprise me to see Cohen named as the next press secretary? Not as much as it should. And Trump would throw him under the bus, first chance he got. Why not? He’s done it before.

Again, the paint is peeling.

Want more sharp takes on politics? Sign up for our free newsletter, Standing Room Only by Amanda Marcotte, also a weekly show on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.

Jokes aside, if I got the opportunity to sit down with Trump, I would treat him with the respect due his office, even though he has done nothing personally to deserve that.I would make clear the interview is for the American public at large, not for my entertainment. I would ask the questions. In a sane world he would provide answers that could facilitate greater understanding of his actions and motivations, and how he believes those actions will benefit the American people. 

Trump’s gift in the past was the ability to sell an alternate reality. He now does that very poorly, and by asking the proper questions we might be able to clarify this country’s predicament — as if many of us haven’t already come to the conclusion that we’re terminally screwed. 

When people get a chance to interview the president — any president, not just this one — the issues and questions should be well researched and precise, in hopes of eliciting responses that are concise and specific. Too much of today’s political discourse consists of “gotcha” moments. Those of us in the press do it. Politicians marinate themselves in it. Trump perfected it. No other president has ever called a reporter “Piggy,” much less gotten away with it.

And if reporters are not playing the gotcha moment, then we are too often serving as propagandists for those in power. Then again, many of us just don’t know how to ask real questions. 

Yeah, the paint is peeling.

What could be more symbolic of the depths of depravity we’ve hit than a president literally giving a paid testimonial on the White House lawn for fertilizer? While the punchlines write themselves, I never had that on my bingo card. I never even imagined such a possibility. It’s a criminal act and an empty and meaningless prostitution of the office. It demeans the entire nation, and adds to the instability in the world.

And what can your average White House reporter do? Not much, beyond watching the turgid, disconcerting vomitorium we call politics with a jaundiced eye, careful of the manipulations and machinations of those who are out to feed their own greed while screwing the rest of us into the ground. It helps if we can laugh about it. 

As we can clearly see this week, the paint is peeling and we have no way to fix it. 

Can I interest you in some fertilizer? Everybody needs “happy grass.”
news.summary: Republicans control DC and have totally wrecked the place. Now the paint is peeling off their delusions

news.title: ‘The Moment’: Taming the ‘Brat’ - The Tribune
news.text: In 2024, a lowercase, sans serif “b” in stark black was set against a lurid neon-green slime background of an album cover — and suddenly, Charli XCX was everywhere.For more than a decade, Charli existed in that peculiar pop-star hinterland: too influential to be obscure, too experimental to be fully mainstream, a hitmaker whose fingerprints were everywhere but whose name remained outside pop’s inner sanctum.Then came ‘Brat’, her sixth album, which detonated far beyond music. Its deliberately pedestrian cover, abrasive club-pop, confessional lyrics and aggressively lowercase aesthetic became a meme, a mood, a fashion statement and, eventually, a lifestyle.“Brat summer” invaded social media and politics alike — “kamala (Harris) IS brat” became shorthand; Collins Dictionary crowned “brat” its 2024 Word of the Year. A record about jealousy, female friendship, insecurity and a whole lot of cocaine became the defining pop-cultural vocabulary of the year.And that is where ‘The Moment’, a mockumentary conceived by Charli herself, begins.Could you kill the best thing that has ever happened to you, because it became bigger than you? The answer, in ‘The Moment’, is apparently yes, if your record label has anything to do with it.This deliciously raw, feral, drug-laced film asks what happens when a cult star is swallowed by her own phenomenon. It begins with, photosensitivity be damned, relentless strobing — and never really lets you breathe.Charli plays herself, preparing for the ‘Brat’ tour while her label, Atlantic Records, attempts to stretch a spontaneous cultural eruption into an endless revenue stream. Cue humiliating sponcon: a “What’s in My Bag?” video for Vogue in which she barely knows what is in her bag, while phone cases, Skims shapewear and glasses sit conspicuously ready for their close-up. Every real person and entity is named as-is.There is nowhere to hide, not even behind the fourth wall.Her yes-men buzz around her. Jamie Demetriou’s manager Tim is wonderfully slippery; Rosanna Arquette’s Atlantic executive wants every last drop. The only person guarding Charli’s vision is creative director Celeste (Hailey Benton Gates, magnificent), as the men around her try to sanitise the club rat into something more palatable for a concert film directed by the punchable Johannes Godwin (Alexander Skarsgard).The film’s greatest triumph is its form. Shot through perpetual cigarette and vape smoke, it is exhausting by design. It looks less like a mockumentary than a panic attack with a production budget. Flashing graphics, real news footage and YouTube commentary bleed into restless camerawork and invasive close-ups. Every scene seems at loggerheads with the next, and you feel the pressure of keeping the money flowing and the “moment” alive.Charli — who punctuates every dialogue with a “babe” in her classic Essex cadence — lets herself look insecure, vain, confused and ridiculous. Her stumbles sharpen the joke: the imperfect starlet is the premise.Skarsgard is the film’s most potent comedic weapon, dressed like a white man on a soul-searching journey in Rishikesh and playing mansplaining incarnate as he attempts to make ‘Brat’ glitterier and more palatable for Amazon, the studio bank-rolling the concert doc. Cameos by Rachel Sennott, Julia Fox and Kylie Jenner add fizz.‘The Moment’ is truly raw and subversive — and, crucially, just fully enough.Perhaps that is the joke. The woman who gave us ‘Brat’ has made a film about what happens when the party ends — and discovered that the comedown is considerably less fun.‘Brat’ was a cultural explosion. ‘The Moment’ is the morning after: mascara smudged, phone buzzing, PR team panicking, everyone pretending they had a great time.

news.title: As midterms near, grocery prices remain top of mind for many Americans
news.text:
PEEKSKILL, New York -- Doreen Hodge didn’t initially plan to shop at a discount supermarket Monday afternoon. But the Peekskill, New York, resident said making the trip to a low-price retailer was worth it given the current cost of food.

"Grocery prices are high everywhere," Hodge told ABC News. "I just actually came here to see if something I wanted to buy was lower."

The cost of food was one of the centerpieces of the 2024 presidential cycle -- and remains a key issue as the midterm election nears.

Two years ago this week, while seeking a second term in the White House, then-candidate Donald Trump spoke in front of his country club in Bedminster, New Jersey, with multiple name-brand food products on display. Standing between two tables full of food store items such as cereal, deli meat, milk, eggs, baby formula and bread, Trump called out then-President Joe Biden and then-Vice President Kamala Harris over the rising cost of everyday grocery items.

"Young people are being devastated by what they’ve done to our country. Grocery prices have skyrocketed," Trump said at the time.

Data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics shows that grocery prices nationwide rose 2.7% over the year ending in July, the most recent month on record, which amounts to triple the year-over-year grocery inflation at the time of Trump’s 2024 address in Bedminster.

Food prices remain top of mind for many Americans. An Associated Press-NORC poll released in early August found that two-thirds of adults disapprove of Trump's handling of the economy.

That same poll found that 41% of Americans said they were concerned about being able to afford groceries over the next few months, up from 24% in April. Nearly half of Americans said the cost of groceries was a major source of stress.

Shopper frustration is more complicated than a glance at the latest inflation data, however, since many people react to an accumulated change in prices on store shelves, David Ortega, a food economist at Michigan State University, told ABC News.

Over a five-year stretch since a pandemic-induced bout of acute inflation, grocery prices have increased more than 20%, most of which took place between 2021 and 2022, a period when Biden occupied the White House, U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data shows.

Outrage among consumers stems in part from the impact of those long-term price increases, in addition to a rekindling of grocery inflation since Trump took office, according to Ortega.

"The reality is the price level today is significantly higher than it was pre-COVID," he said.

“We were able to make a lot of progress in bringing that rate of inflation for food down, but what we’ve seen in the past couple of years is food inflation has started to pick up again,” Ortega added.

And shoppers are noticing.

"We’re spending a lot of money but leaving with smaller bags," shopper Aaron Thevenin told ABC News while leaving a grocery store in West Haverstraw, New York.

"You spend like almost double what you were planning to spend," Lori Tetro of Cortlandt Manor, New York, said.

Peekskill, West Haverstraw and Cortlandt Manor all sit within New York’s 17th Congressional District, an area covering multiple suburbs north of New York City that is split relatively evenly between Democrats and Republicans.

Control of Congress could come down to districts like the 17th, which is currently represented by Republican Rep. Mike Lawler. He has co-introduced a number of bipartisan grocery-related bills during his time in Congress, including the Lower Grocery Prices Act in 2025 and the No Rigged Grocery Prices Act in May.

Cait Conley, the Democratic candidate who is taking on Lawler in the 17th District, is pointing to rising supermarket bills as one of the reasons why voters should consider flipping the seat.

"You’re watching families have to make tradeoffs between filling up the grocery cart and the gas tank," Conley told ABC News.

House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Republican, said Monday that Trump is "laser focused on bringing down the cost for everybody" and that he hopes that a coalition of nations working together to help resolve the war in Iran will lower grocery prices.

The White House, in a statement to ABC News on Thursday, said that the president has "implemented policies that have brought prices of key essentials ranging from prescription drugs to eggs to auto insurance down in historic ways."

"The Administration remains focused on delivering more relief for American families, and as traffic through the Strait of Hormuz normalizes, energy prices -- and thus overall inflation -- will continue cooling again," White House spokesman Kush Desai said in the statement.

The Trump administration issued a statement in early August noting that "private sector companies are responding to President Trump's call by delivering tangible price reductions on everyday goods and services — putting money back in the pockets of American workers and families."

To Americans like Hodge, high grocery prices are continuing to shape their everyday shopping decisions.

"It’s terrible, but you do what you have to do," Hodge said. "We all have to eat."
news.summary: While campaigning in 2024, President Donald Trump promised to lower grocery prices, but many Americans are still having a hard time affording the cost of food.

Food prices remain top of mind for many Americans. An Associated Press-NORC poll released in early August found that two-thirds of adults disapprove of Trump's handling of the economy.

That same poll found that 41% of Americans said they were concerned about being able to afford groceries over the next few months, up from 24% in April. Nearly half of Americans said the cost of groceries was a major source of stress.

Shopper frustration is more complicated than a glance at the latest inflation data, however, since many people react to an accumulated change in prices on store shelves, David Ortega, a food economist at Michigan State University, told ABC News.

Over a five-year stretch since a pandemic-induced bout of acute inflation, grocery prices have increased more than 20%, most of which took place between 2021 and 2022, a period when Biden occupied the White House, U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data shows.

Outrage among consumers stems in part from the impact of those long-term price increases, in addition to a rekindling of grocery inflation since Trump took office, according to Ortega.

"The reality is the price level today is significantly higher than it was pre-COVID," he said.

“We were able to make a lot of progress in bringing that rate of inflation for food down, but what we’ve seen in the past couple of years is food inflation has started to pick up again,” Ortega added.

And shoppers are noticing.

"We’re spending a lot of money but leaving with smaller bags," shopper Aaron Thevenin told ABC News while leaving a grocery store in West Haverstraw, New York.

"You spend like almost double what you were planning to spend," Lori Tetro of Cortlandt Manor, New York, said.

Peekskill, West Haverstraw and Cortlandt Manor all sit within New York’s 17th Congressional District, an area covering multiple suburbs north of New York City that is split relatively evenly between Democrats and Republicans.

Control of Congress could come down to districts like the 17th, which is currently represented by Republican Rep. Mike Lawler. He has co-introduced a number of bipartisan grocery-related bills during his time in Congress, including the Lower Grocery Prices Act in 2025 and the No Rigged Grocery Prices Act in May.

Cait Conley, the Democratic candidate who is taking on Lawler in the 17th District, is pointing to rising supermarket bills as one of the reasons why voters should consider flipping the seat.

"You’re watching families have to make tradeoffs between filling up the grocery cart and the gas tank," Conley told ABC News.

House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Republican, said Monday that Trump is "laser focused on bringing down the cost for everybody" and that he hopes that a coalition of nations working together to help resolve the war in Iran will lower grocery prices.

The White House, in a statement to ABC News on Thursday, said that the president has "implemented policies that have brought prices of key essentials ranging from prescription drugs to eggs to auto insurance down in historic ways."

"The Administration remains focused on delivering more relief for American families, and as traffic through the Strait of Hormuz normalizes, energy prices -- and thus overall inflation -- will continue cooling again," White House spokesman Kush Desai said in the statement.

The Trump administration issued a statement in early August noting that "private sector companies are responding to President Trump's call by delivering tangible price reductions on everyday goods and services — putting money back in the pockets of American workers and families."

To Americans like Hodge, high grocery prices are continuing to shape their everyday shopping decisions.

"It’s terrible, but you do what you have to do," Hodge said. "We all have to eat."
news.summary: While campaigning in 2024, President Donald Trump promised to lower grocery prices, but many Americans are still having a hard time affording the cost of food.
news.author: Jared Kofsky And Max Zahn,San Francisco

news.text:
Far-right influencer Laura Loomer was hit with a series of troubling allegations this week in a lawsuit filed against the Trump administration, the plaintiff of which accused Loomer of being an “unregistered” foreign lobbyist.

On Thursday, The Grayzone revealed that its editor, Max Blumenthal, had filed a lawsuit against Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin after Blumenthal’s phones were seized by U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents last month. The lawsuit was filed by the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee, and alleges that the Trump administration violated Blumenthal’s First and Fourth Amendment rights at the direction of Loomer.

“Was the order to seize my devices delivered under pressure from unregistered Israel and Ukraine lobbyist Laura Loomer, who boasted about calling Trump cabinet officials to demand I be jailed for my reporting from Iran, and effectively took credit for the confiscation of my devices?” Blumenthal asked Thursday evening in a social media post on X.

“We're filing this lawsuit to answer that question, and to prevent the unconstitutional weaponization of federal law enforcement against journalists whose reporting complicates their malign, Israeli-directed agenda.”

As cited in the lawsuit, Loomer had led an aggressive and public campaign against Blumenthal in response to the journalist having traveled to Iran to report on the funeral of former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. 

In one social media post, Loomer urged Mullin to have Blumenthal “taken off the plane by US Marshalls when he lands back in the US” and “revoke his passport.” In another, she urged the FBI to conduct a “heavily armed raid” on his home at 5 a.m. After Blumenthal’s phones were seized, she indicated she had insider knowledge of the FBI’s interest in him.

While Loomer has no official position within the Trump administration, she wielded “breathtaking influence” in the White House, having played an outsized role in the administration’s mass firings and immigration policies.

A self-described “proud Islamophobe,” Loomer has a long history of making what critics have labeled as overtly racist and bigoted remarks, particularly against Muslims, having called them “savages.” Her racially charged remarks have also been extended to other ethnicities, including Indians, with Loomer once warning that the White House would “smell like curry” if former Vice President Kamala Harris – whose mother was Indian – won the 2024 presidential election.

news.title: Ariana Grande Rages at Trump for Using Her Song in Trans-Trolling TikTok Post
news.text:
An underwhelmed Ariana Grande raged against President Donald Trump on Thursday for using her song in a trans-trolling TikTok post, cautioning him to “Never use my music again,” before sternly adding, “Also, your truth is false.”

The three-time Grammy winner chose to unleash as she comes to the end days of her Eternal Sunshine Tour.

The public admonition was sparked by a TikTok video posted by the Trump campaign, which used Grande’s 2024 single We Can’t Be Friends (Wait for Your Love) to affirm the reality that men are men and women are women and neither sex represents an interchangeable option.

“Me and my truth we sit in silence… men can’t have babies and should never compete in women’s sports,” the post read alongside the caption: “This shouldn’t be controversial!”

 @teamtrump 
This shouldn’t be controversial! #trump #arianagrande #maga
 ♬ original sound – Amina Kaddachi 

Grande appeared in the comments to tell the Trump administration to back off, “Never use my music again.”

This is not the first time the singer has been at odds with the White House.

As Breitbart News reported back in June, Trump’s media team used Grande’s song Bye in a video showing ICE agents arresting illegal aliens and the left-wing pop star was not happy about it.

Grande’s immediately told the Trump administration to cease and desist. “Please do not ever use my music in relation to this barbaric, inhumane, heinous nonsense. Fck ice,” she huffed in her comment.

The sound was stripped from the clip shortly after Ariana Grande unleashed her political spray – as is her increasing custom.

In the past she supported Kamala Harris for president and performed for former President Barack Obama at the White House in 2014.

The Wicked actress joins a growing list of sensitive artists who have demanded Trump’s team do not use their music to promote the president’s policy agenda.

Last year, Sabrina Carpenter wrote “do not ever involve me or my music to benefit your inhumane agenda” after a White House clip used part of her 2024 song Juno in a compilation showing ICE operations.

ABBA, Céline Dion and Beyoncé were among those demanding Trump’s campaign not use their music during his successful re-election bid in 2024, including at campaign rallies.

news.title: At the Iowa State Fair, pork chops mix with presidential politics. Will that change?
news.text:
Tucked in amid the funnel cake stands and livestock exhibits is a small trailer decorated with bright images of fruit. Hoppy’s Lemonade Shake-Up, one of the Iowa State Fair’s oldest and most beloved vendors, has been selling lemonade to thirsty fairgoers for 79 years. 

Dana Hartney has worked at Hoppy’s for decades. “I love everything about it,” she says. “I've spent my entire life coming out here.” 

Former Massachusetts Sen. John Kerry once bought a lemonade here, Ms. Hartney recalls. So did Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders. More recently, she met Joe Biden during his successful 2020 presidential campaign. “I said, ‘Hey, Joe,’ and he said, ‘Hey,’ and I got a whole picture of him waving at me. I was starstruck.”

One of the longest-running summer attractions in America, the Iowa State Fair has been a mainstay for generations of Iowans – and politicians. For half a century, scores of White House hopefuls have come to the fairgrounds just east of Des Moines to flip pork chops and shake hands, trying to generate buzz. 

But while much of the fair seems almost impervious to change – from its famous butter sculptures to the astonishing array of food items on sticks – its place in the pantheon of presidential politics might be waning.

Until recently, Iowa held first-in-the-nation caucuses for both major parties, making the Midwestern state a key proving ground. A win here or even a better-than-expected performance could give a candidate crucial momentum heading into New Hampshire and the primary states that followed. 

In the 2024 election cycle, however, the Democratic National Committee stripped Iowa of its early voting status – a response to technical mishaps that had marred the 2020 caucuses, as well as complaints that Iowa’s heavily white, rural population was not representative of the Democratic base. 

The change didn’t particularly matter that year, as then-President Biden was essentially running unopposed for the party’s nomination. (He later stepped aside, and Vice President Kamala Harris became the nominee.) But in 2028, when the race is likely to be wide-open, the Democratic primary calendar will be far more impactful – and, again, Iowa will not be voting first. The DNC voted on Aug. 15 to make South Carolina the first primary state, followed by Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan, and Virginia.

Iowa Democrats have registered their disapproval. “I’m deeply concerned that our party has not learned from past mistakes. We need a [Midwestern] and a truly rural state to be among the first four states,” said Rita Hart, the Iowa Democratic Party chair, when she voted against the new calendar at the DNC’s summer meeting. 

Iowa will still go first for Republicans – which means the state fair will continue to be a prominent stop for potential GOP candidates. But if Democratic candidates stop coming, it would mark something of the end of an era. Every president since Ronald Reagan has flipped a chop at the Iowa Pork Producers Association.

In 2007, after then-Sen. Barack Obama likened Southern Illinois to Iowa, a mistake so grievous that Politico columnist Roger Simon predicted it would doom his campaign, he advised Mr. Obama to “go to the Iowa State Fair and eat stuff. Lots of stuff.”

Mr. Obama, of course, went on to win the Iowa caucuses – and to win Iowa in the general election, the last Democrat to do so. 

Notably, after swinging to the right during the post-Obama era, the state suddenly has a slate of competitive races this year, including contests for an open Senate seat and the governorship. That alone could give some national Democrats a reason to keep coming to the fair. 

Earlier this month, Trump administration officials, including Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, dropped by. So did Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona, who has said he’s considering a presidential run.

“We'll see if Republicans manage to hold on to all of these races, and [Iowa] continues to be on the red side of purple. Then, maybe Democrats won't be as interested,” says Tim Hagle, a political science professor at the University of Iowa. “But if all of a sudden they say, ‘Hey, we've got some hope here. We've got a chance of maybe winning Iowa in the general election,’ then we're going to see those people show up.”

Certainly, Iowans hope the attention and access they’ve gotten over the years won’t come to an end. One couple sitting near the Political Soapbox, where candidates come to deliver their pitches, has camped in the same spot for the past 28 years with friends and family. 

“It's kind of like our own little village when we're here,” says Lynne, who asked to use her middle name because she works for the state.

“There would be times I would hoof it down” to see candidates like Mr. Obama, Mr. Biden, or then-candidate Donald Trump after his helicopter arrival, she says. Lynne’s husband was standing in line one day and glanced over his shoulder to see former House Speaker Newt Gingrich standing right behind him.

“It really is pretty exciting to have someone of that stature come,” she says.
news.summary: The state fair in Des Moines has been a mainstay for generations of Iowans – and for White House hopefuls. But some worry its place in the pantheon of presidential politics might be waning.
news.author: Sophie Hills
